title: Grid lines, crossings and coordinates
transcript: A grid is made from lines, spaces between the lines, and points where the lines meet. These are three different things to count. For a rectangle on a grid, choose the two lines that form each pair of opposite edges.

An AMC Upper Primary question can ask for intersections, paths, or shapes cut out by grid lines. Mark the object being counted. A Rossmoyne style grid problem can require a shape to include one marked cell while avoiding another. Count by the possible boundaries.
The grid has six columns and three rows of squares. How many points where vertical and horizontal lines meet are there? Count the lines along the outside edges too.
six columns need seven vertical lines. three rows need four horizontal lines. Each vertical line crosses all four horizontal lines. Multiply to get twenty-eight crossing points.
A sheet has four columns and six rows of cells. Count all rectangles whose sides lie along its grid lines. Rectangles can have any size. A square counts too.

Choose two of the five vertical lines. An unordered pair makes the left and right edge. There are ten choices. There are twenty-one horizontal pairs. Choose one vertical pair and one horizontal pair independently. The four selected lines specify a unique rectangle. Multiply the counts to get two hundred and ten.

On a grid with six columns and six rows, cell A is in column three, row three. Rows are numbered from the bottom. Cell B is in column six, row four. Count the grid-line rectangles containing all of A but none of the interior of B. One way to begin is to count every rectangle containing A. Then identify the unwanted ones.

To contain A, the left and right edges have three and four choices respectively. The lower and upper edges have three and four choices. That is one hundred and forty-four rectangles. Each rectangle is counted once by the locations of its four sides. Now require it to contain both cells. Each side must sit outside the smallest block that contains A and B.

The edge counts for a rectangle enclosing both are three, one, three and three. Their product is twenty-seven. Subtract those from the count containing A. Exactly one hundred and seventeen rectangles contain A and avoid B.

The outside boundary contributes two edge lines in each direction. A row of five cells sits between six lines. For a rectangle, the pair of left and right lines has no order to choose twice. Choosing the lines fixes their order automatically.

Mark whether you are choosing lines, crossing points or cells. Count the outer boundaries before using a formula. Set constraints on one edge choice at a time. For a cell to be excluded, subtract exactly the choices that include it.
